findings.issue_text: ClientPermissionsV2.canExchangeTo throws UnsupportedOperationException, so every client-to-client token exchange in a V2 deployment (via DefaultTokenExchangeProvider calling AdminPermissions.management().clients().canExchangeTo) returns a 500 instead of being evaluated or denied

ClientPermissionsV2.isPermissionsEnabled and setPermissionsEnabled throw, causing the /admin/realms/{realm}/clients/{id}/management/permissions GET and PUT endpoints to return 500 under V2, and causing client deletion to fail via the ClientRemovedEvent listener when both V1 and V2 features are enabled

AdminPermissions ClientRemovedEvent listener is gated entirely on the V1 feature flag, so in a V2-only deployment deleting a client leaves its Resource and attached scope permissions orphaned in the admin-permissions resource server (and same for roles/groups once V2 supports them)

ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission(ClientModel, String) falls back to getResourceTypeResource(...) and dereferences the result without a null check (in findByResource and resource.getScopes()), causing an NPE for realms whose admin-permissions resource server was initialised before the 'Clients' type existed; the scope-only overload null-checks the same lookup, so the paths are inconsistent

ClientPermissionsV2.canView(client) chains canView(), canConfigure(client), canManage(client), and its own hasPermission, each running a full policy evaluation, so a single view check can cost up to four evaluations and the client list endpoint runs this per client

Javadoc for ClientPermissionEvaluator.requireView() and requireViewClientScopes() says 'Returns true if ...' but both are void methods that throw ForbiddenException; should match the wording on the other require* methods
ClientPermissionsV2.getEvaluationContext and the logger field are never referenced (dead code), suggesting the token-exchange evaluation was planned but never wired up

PermissionClientTest has no test coverage for MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE, a single-client VIEW permission, Logic.NEGATIVE on a client permission overriding an all-clients grant, or getClientsWithPermission, leaving the client type less covered than the user tests

PermissionClientTest.testManageOnlyOneClient removes getDefaultClientScopes().get(1) from 'myclient' (the OAuth client the test admin authenticates through) using an order-dependent index and never restores it, so later tests in the class could receive tokens missing a default scope

goldens.comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.

In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.

In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.

In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called

adjudication_records.issue_text: ClientPermissionsV2.canExchangeTo throws UnsupportedOperationException, so every client-to-client token exchange in a V2 deployment (via DefaultTokenExchangeProvider calling AdminPermissions.management().clients().canExchangeTo) returns a 500 instead of being evaluated or denied

adjudication.rationale: The diff does show `ClientPermissionsV2.canExchangeTo(...)` unconditionally throwing `UnsupportedOperationException("Not supported in V2")`. However, the finding’s key claim—that *DefaultTokenExchangeProvider* (or any token-exchange path) calls `AdminPermissions.management().clients().canExchangeTo` in a V2 deployment, resulting in a 500 for “every client-to-client token exchange”—is not evidenced anywhere in this PR diff (no token-exchange provider changes/call sites are shown, nor any wiring proving this method is invoked under V2). So the stated end-to-end broken behavior cannot be verified from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: ClientPermissionsV2.isPermissionsEnabled and setPermissionsEnabled throw, causing the /admin/realms/{realm}/clients/{id}/management/permissions GET and PUT endpoints to return 500 under V2, and causing client deletion to fail via the ClientRemovedEvent listener when both V1 and V2 features are enabled

adjudication.rationale: In the new `ClientPermissionsV2` class, both `isPermissionsEnabled(ClientModel)` and `setPermissionsEnabled(ClientModel, boolean)` are overridden to throw `UnsupportedOperationException` ("Not supported in V2"). The diff also shows the `AdminPermissions.registerListener` `ClientRemovedEvent` handler calling `management(...).clients().setPermissionsEnabled(cast.getClient(), false)` when `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ` is enabled. Since `MgmtPermissionsV2.clients()` now returns `ClientPermissionsV2`, a `ClientRemovedEvent` under V2 can trigger this throwing method, which would break client deletion/event handling (likely surfacing as a 500/error). The claim about the specific REST endpoints returning 500 is plausible given the method contract, but the event-listener failure is directly verifiable from the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: ClientPermissionsV2.canView(client) chains canView(), canConfigure(client), canManage(client), and its own hasPermission, each running a full policy evaluation, so a single view check can cost up to four evaluations and the client list endpoint runs this per client

adjudication.rationale: In `ClientPermissionsV2.canView(ClientModel client)`, the control flow can trigger multiple independent `hasPermission(...)` calls, each of which does `root.evaluatePermission(new ResourcePermission(...))` (a full policy evaluation). Specifically: `canView(client)` calls `canView()` (which may call `hasPermission(AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW)`), then `canConfigure(client)` (which may call `canManage(client)` -> `hasPermission(client, MANAGE)` and then `hasPermission(client, CONFIGURE)`), and finally falls back to `hasPermission(client, VIEW)`. This is up to 4 separate evaluations for a single view check in the worst case. This is a concrete, diff-grounded performance/architecture concern, not a correctness defect. The claim about the client list endpoint doing this per client is plausible but not directly shown in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Javadoc for ClientPermissionEvaluator.requireView() and requireViewClientScopes() says 'Returns true if ...' but both are void methods that throw ForbiddenException; should match the wording on the other require* methods

adjudication.rationale: In ClientPermissionEvaluator, the new Javadocs for requireView() and requireViewClientScopes() indeed say “Returns true if …” while both methods are declared void (and, by convention with other require* methods, throw ForbiddenException). However, this is only a documentation wording inconsistency; the diff does not show any functional defect or behavioral break caused by it.

adjudication_records.issue_text: PermissionClientTest has no test coverage for MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE, a single-client VIEW permission, Logic.NEGATIVE on a client permission overriding an all-clients grant, or getClientsWithPermission, leaving the client type less covered than the user tests

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds new client-related scopes and logic (e.g., AdminPermissionsSchema.MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE / VIEW scope evaluation and ClientPermissionsV2#getClientsWithPermission), and PermissionClientTest only adds coverage for MANAGE, CONFIGURE, MAP_ROLES, and MAP_ROLES_COMPOSITE (see tests testManageOnlyOneClient, testConfigureOnlyOneClient, testManageAllClients, testViewAllClients, testMapRolesAndCompositesOnlyOneClient). There is no test exercising MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE, no test for a single-client VIEW-only grant, no test for Logic.NEGATIVE on a client permission overriding an all-clients grant, and no test hitting getClientsWithPermission. This is a concrete coverage gap for newly introduced behavior, not a proven runtime defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: PermissionClientTest.testManageOnlyOneClient removes getDefaultClientScopes().get(1) from 'myclient' (the OAuth client the test admin authenticates through) using an order-dependent index and never restores it, so later tests in the class could receive tokens missing a default scope

adjudication.rationale: In `PermissionClientTest.testManageOnlyOneClient`, the test fetches `myclient` (the same client used by `@InjectAdminClient(..., client = "myclient", ...)`) and then permanently mutates its configuration by calling `clientResource.removeDefaultClientScope(clientScopeRep.getId())` where `clientScopeRep` is selected via `getDefaultClientScopes().get(1)` (order-dependent). The class `@AfterEach` only deletes created permissions (`permissions.findAll(...).remove()`), and does not restore the removed default client scope, so this side effect can leak into later tests in the class (and the index-based selection itself is brittle).
